runs.text: Travis Kim
Confetti

“Mr Capaldi believed there was nothing special inside Josie...He told the Mother he’d searched and searched and found nothing...But I believe...he was searching in the wrong place. There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie. It was inside those who loved her.”
-Kazuo Ishiguro

I didn’t have any memories when I started here. It was hard to remember anything anyways, doing the same thing every day. At first, they didn't want me working up front. I would come in after the pairings and sweep. Sweeping was my life for a while, but it wasn't as bad as it sounds. I was curious about the pairings. I could tell a lot about who was paired by the remains: the family photographs left to be forgotten, the thick crust of a sweet-potato pie, the shoes of the far-too-drunk.

As I swept, I found great joy in uncovering my treasures. People always lose things. It seems the more they enjoy themselves, the less they care about what they used to have. I wasn't supposed to keep anything I swept, but nobody ever checked. I had a box in my quarters, one I found and used to store the little things. A lost earring or an unburnt candle. Here and there I would uncover a little more. If anything, I wanted to discover what it meant to be human. To one day have a pairing of my own.

Humans are always smiling, at least that's all I saw. But I read somewhere that humans can still be sad when they smile. They're not programmed like us—to never lie. Even so, we were the ones forgotten. It never really made me sad or anything, but it was hard at times to be ignored. I found it funny that they would give up so much to find somebody to understand and accept them, but they couldn't do either to us. But I guess we weren't fully human, being only modeled and modified off of them.

So I was stuck with being loved through sweeping. Every now and then, especially with the older pairings, they'd leave some cash on the tables. I found that odd, that they would think to pay me. Still, it pleased me because it meant they had considered their remains, even though I had no use for the money. I loved them then. The remains.

The one thing I didn’t enjoy cleaning was confetti. I don't like confetti. Confetti is a mess, the colors fade, and I was always left with thousands of strips of plastic and paper littering the ground and walls. The thing with confetti is you have to sweep the opposite way. Usually you

pull the broom in towards you, but confetti has this annoying staticky property that leaves it stuck to every surface. Instead you push the broom away from you, as you purge their leering presence, one at a time. People always left confetti. Later, when I was able to stay during the pairings, I saw confetti before it touched the ground. After the pairings agreed, the family launched it everywhere, and as it rained to the ground, I understood its aesthetic purpose. How could you believe in love if not for the beauty and value in the things not necessary?

Sweeping the confetti was tedious, as if I was pushing away a piece of myself each time. Push, heave, extend my arms forward, joint by joint, step by step, slowly expelling the uncaring remains. I thought of the understanding. That's what I read, that love was supposed to be unconditional and understanding, but in these moments, the more I tried to love the humans that had created me, the more I felt I was misunderstood. For they had found their love through the applications; surely they had the capacity to understand, but not for me.

We weren't made to feel emotions. I had never felt truly happy or sad, at least not in the momentous ways humans seemed to, but sweeping confetti, it was a terribly lonely feeling. I guess they hadn't thought of that.

I tried filling out an application once, with an identity I made up and all. It didn't make it past the first round. I guess they had some sort of safeguard against artificials. It was around that time that they promoted me. I was working at the desk now, meeting people, matching their smiles, and ignoring their remains. For a while, I didn't think much about my old job. I was good at my new one; I rarely made mistakes, and clients were always happy. But technology was always improving, and after they got the new models, I was back to sweeping.

The thing with pairings is that even after such an extensive application and review process, the final match didn't always work. Some little thing—visible only in person, left out in words and feeling, but clear in their omission—cut the pairing short, even with confetti flying through the air. It was on these days that I felt the worst. Nothing had been done and the confetti's beauty was
lost.

It was always an uncomfortable ordeal when the pairings ended early, so people left as soon as they could. I rushed in then, hoping to end the ugliness as fast as possible. The last time I did that, when I started sweeping from the far corner, I had the sickening notion that someone was still in the room. If I wasn't alone, then any treasure I found wouldn't be mine to interpret. So partly out of curiosity and partly out of despair, I turned my head to see a figure wiping the table closest to the door, scrubbing with extra ferocity at the stained tablecloth.

She called out to me, asking if I needed any help. I was too flustered to answer, never having been asked that question, never having been asked any question for that matter besides "where's the bathroom?" Recollecting myself, I answered with my gratitude, saying that I needed no help, that she should go with her family. By even staying, I had finally met someone I could relate to

the remains. I was more than thankful. But she was adamant that she would stay and help, that she would try to understand because “clearly the other guy couldn't, Jeez, what’s wrong with people these days.” I realized that she was the one who had called off the pairing.

So we pushed and scrubbed and pulled and swept, the food from the tables and the confetti from the floor. My world seemed lighter, as I realized I was being heard through my work. So even when she left, I cherished that moment. For a while, confetti was no trouble to me.

To nobody’s surprise I began to fade around then. At that point, my decline had been due for a couple months. We weren't meant to last very long because that's how the companies made money. You had to buy a new
artificial
after a while.

I was often left in my quarters, left to remember the little things, opening up my little box to inspect and remember my treasure. I would thumb through the items, my vision fading, feeling the coins, the earrings, the seeds, and that one strip of colored plastic, the one that had been stuck to her sweater, letting go only as she stepped out the door.
I thought to myself then, that I had been happy.
It was the confetti that she left behind, the strip of yellow glued to my heart, which convinced me. I had been pessimistic, many times ago and many times
current

. But hope is a powerful feeling, and she had given it to me. To realize that even though the understanding which brought us together had the same staticky property as confetti, it was not evil. It was what she left behind, and it was beautiful.
Consider your remains—the things left behind—because someone will sweep them and someone will treasure them. The nature of the discarded is that it will one day become new again.
Inspired by the novel
Klara and the Sun
by Kazuo Ishiguro.
